title: Programming Language Release Atlas
description: Selected language and platform release lines, editions and standards. Dates describe public releases or standard editions, not direct code inheritance.

curriculumPresets.title: Full programming atlas
curriculumPresets.description: Compare release cadence, language editions, runtimes and standardisation models across the complete map.

curriculumPresets.title: Software development choices
curriculumPresets.description: Compare current Python, C#, Java, TypeScript, Rust, Go, Kotlin, PHP and Swift lines. Justify a language choice using purpose, ecosystem and support status.

curriculumPresets.title: Standards versus implementations
curriculumPresets.description: Contrast ISO C and C++ editions, Java/OpenJDK releases and vendor-led languages. Explain why a standard and an implementation are not interchangeable.

curriculumPresets.title: Web programming stack
curriculumPresets.description: Trace JavaScript, TypeScript and PHP releases, then identify which code executes in a browser, server or build tool.

curriculumPresets.title: Systems programming
curriculumPresets.description: Compare the C, C++, Rust and Go branches. Investigate memory safety, concurrency and compatibility without assuming newer means suitable for every task.

curriculumPresets.title: Data and scientific programming
curriculumPresets.description: Compare R, Julia and Python release ecosystems, then design a reproducibility record covering interpreter, packages, data and environment.

curriculumPresets.title: Functional programming ideas
curriculumPresets.description: Use Haskell, Scala and Clojure to investigate purity, immutable data, type systems and hosted runtimes.

curriculumPresets.title: Shell and automation
curriculumPresets.description: Compare Bash and PowerShell pipelines, quoting, error handling and cross-platform deployment risks.

nodes.name: Programming Languages
nodes.note: Languages evolve through standards, vendor releases, open-source governance and runtime ecosystems. Lines here show selected milestones rather than every version.
nodes.hook: Choose two branches and explain whether their numbered releases represent specifications, implementations or both.

nodes.name: Python
nodes.note: Python uses numbered language releases implemented primarily through CPython.
nodes.hook: Trace one Python feature through the What’s New index and test whether old code remains valid.

nodes.name: Python 2.0
nodes.note: Python 2 established the historical line later separated from Python 3.
nodes.hook: Explain why migration between major versions may require code changes.

nodes.name: Python 3.0
nodes.note: Python 3 deliberately revised incompatible language behaviour.
nodes.hook: Find one Python 2 to 3 incompatibility and describe its maintenance cost.

nodes.name: Python 3.14.7
nodes.note: A current maintenance release in the 3.14 series.
nodes.hook: Check the release page and separate security, bug-fix and language-feature changes.

nodes.name: Python 3.15 RC1
nodes.note: A release candidate for Python 3.15, not the final production release.
nodes.hook: Explain why a team might test against an RC but avoid deploying it.

nodes.name: Java and JVM
nodes.note: Java language releases are closely connected to JVM and JDK implementations.
nodes.hook: Distinguish the Java language, JVM and JDK in a deployment diagram.

nodes.name: Java / JDK 8
nodes.note: JDK 8 is an influential long-lived release line.
nodes.hook: Investigate why long-term-support policies affect enterprise upgrade timing.

nodes.name: JDK 17
nodes.note: JDK 17 is a later long-term-support reference point in many distributions.
nodes.hook: Compare language features with runtime and library changes.

nodes.name: JDK 21
nodes.note: JDK 21 is another widely adopted long-term-support line.
nodes.hook: Create an upgrade risk register from JDK 17 to 21.

nodes.name: JDK 26
nodes.note: JDK 26 reached general availability on 17 March 2026.
nodes.hook: Use the project page to classify final, preview and incubator features.

nodes.name: JDK 27 RC
nodes.note: JDK 27 was at release-candidate status when checked.
nodes.hook: Explain what evidence would justify changing this node to released.

nodes.name: C# and .NET
nodes.note: C# language versions are delivered with .NET SDK and compiler support.
nodes.hook: Map source language, compiler, runtime and libraries for one C# application.

nodes.name: C# 1.0
nodes.note: The first standardised C# release established the managed-language line.
nodes.hook: Compare managed execution with native compilation at a high level.

nodes.name: C# 8.0
nodes.note: C# 8 introduced a major modern feature set including nullable reference types.
nodes.hook: Assess how compiler analysis can reduce defects without changing runtime data.

nodes.name: C# 12
nodes.note: C# 12 shipped with .NET 8.
nodes.hook: Identify which project settings select a language version.

nodes.name: C# 14
nodes.note: C# 14 is the current language version supported on .NET 10.
nodes.hook: Evaluate whether one C# 14 feature improves readability or only shortens syntax.

nodes.name: JavaScript / ECMAScript
nodes.note: JavaScript implementations track the ECMAScript specification and host environments.
nodes.hook: Separate language features from browser APIs in a short code sample.

nodes.name: ECMAScript 5
nodes.note: ES5 was a major compatibility baseline for modern JavaScript.
nodes.hook: Find an ES5 feature still common in current code.

nodes.name: ECMAScript 2015
nodes.note: ES2015 began annual edition naming and delivered major syntax and module changes.
nodes.hook: Classify one feature as syntax, semantics or module organisation.

nodes.name: ECMAScript 2026
nodes.note: The 2026 edition sits within ECMAScript’s annual standardisation cycle.
nodes.hook: Use the live specification and proposals process to distinguish standard from proposal.

nodes.name: TypeScript
nodes.note: TypeScript extends JavaScript syntax with static type checking and compiles to JavaScript.
nodes.hook: Draw the path from TypeScript source to JavaScript execution.

nodes.name: TypeScript 5.x
nodes.note: The 5.x line developed the established compiler before major 2026 releases.
nodes.hook: Compare language service benefits with emitted JavaScript.

nodes.name: TypeScript 6.0
nodes.note: TypeScript 6.0 was released on 23 March 2026.
nodes.hook: Read the migration notes and identify one potential breaking change.

nodes.name: TypeScript 7.0
nodes.note: TypeScript 7.0 was released on 8 July 2026.
nodes.hook: Compare the 6.0 and 7.0 announcements, focusing on compiler architecture and migration.

nodes.name: Systems Languages
nodes.note: C, C++, Rust and Go illustrate different approaches to performance, safety and concurrency.
nodes.hook: Select a systems task and defend one language choice against two alternatives.

nodes.name: C89 / C90
nodes.note: Early ISO standardisation provided a portable baseline for C.
nodes.hook: Explain why decades-old C standards remain relevant to toolchains.

nodes.name: C11
nodes.note: C11 extended the standard with concurrency and other facilities.
nodes.hook: Investigate which C11 features depend on compiler and library support.

nodes.name: C23
nodes.note: C23 is the latest published ISO C revision in this selected line.
nodes.hook: Compare a C23 change with its earlier compiler extension.

nodes.name: C++98
nodes.note: C++98 was the first ISO C++ standard.
nodes.hook: Describe how C++ relates historically to C without calling it a simple replacement.

nodes.name: C++11
nodes.note: C++11 substantially modernised the language and standard library.
nodes.hook: Find one C++11 feature that changed common coding style.

nodes.name: C++23
nodes.note: C++23 is the current published standard while C++26 work continues.
nodes.hook: Separate published-standard features from C++26 proposals.

nodes.name: C++26 work
nodes.note: C++26 is work in progress rather than a published final standard.
nodes.hook: Use proposal status to judge whether production guidance is premature.

nodes.name: Rust
nodes.note: Rust combines native performance goals with compile-time memory-safety checks and explicit editions.
nodes.hook: Contrast a Rust edition with a compiler release.

nodes.name: Rust 2018
nodes.note: The 2018 edition evolved language ergonomics while preserving edition interoperability.
nodes.hook: Explain why editions can coexist in one dependency graph.

nodes.name: Rust 2024 / 1.85
nodes.note: Rust 1.85 stabilised the Rust 2024 edition.
nodes.hook: Identify an edition migration lint and explain its purpose.

nodes.name: Rust 1.98
nodes.note: Rust 1.98 was released on 20 August 2026.
nodes.hook: Classify changes as language, compiler, standard library or tooling.

nodes.name: Go
nodes.note: Go emphasises simple tooling, fast builds and built-in concurrency primitives.
nodes.hook: Compare goroutines with operating-system threads at an appropriate abstraction level.

nodes.name: Go 1
nodes.note: Go 1 established a compatibility promise for the major release line.
nodes.hook: Assess how compatibility promises influence library maintenance.

nodes.name: Go 1.26
nodes.note: Go 1.26 was released on 10 February 2026.
nodes.hook: Use the release notes to identify one compiler and one library change.

nodes.name: Application Languages
nodes.note: Kotlin, PHP and Swift show different platform and application-development paths.
nodes.hook: Match each language to typical runtime and deployment contexts without stereotyping its use.

nodes.name: Kotlin 2.4.10
nodes.note: Kotlin 2.4.10 is the current 2.4 bug-fix release listed by JetBrains.
nodes.hook: Use the support table to distinguish latest, stable and supported.

nodes.name: PHP 8.5
nodes.note: PHP 8.5 is a current server-side language release line.
nodes.hook: Check platform requirements before proposing an upgrade.

nodes.name: Swift 6.3
nodes.note: Swift 6.3 was announced on 24 March 2026.
nodes.hook: Identify one language or tooling change and connect it to an app-development workflow.

nodes.name: Data and Scientific Languages
nodes.note: R and Julia represent different approaches to statistical and technical computing.
nodes.hook: Compare package ecosystems, execution models and reproducibility requirements for one analysis task.

nodes.name: R
nodes.note: R is a language and environment for statistical computing distributed through CRAN.
nodes.hook: Separate the language release, package version and analysis environment in a reproducibility record.

nodes.name: R 1.0
nodes.note: R 1.0 marked a major public release milestone.
nodes.hook: Identify which historical scripts would need package or syntax migration.

nodes.name: R 4.0
nodes.note: R 4.0 began the current major release series.
nodes.hook: Investigate one compatibility change at the 4.0 boundary.

nodes.name: R 4.6.1
nodes.note: R 4.6.1 was the current CRAN release when checked.
nodes.hook: Capture session information and package versions for a repeatable practical.

nodes.name: Julia
nodes.note: Julia targets technical computing with a high-level language and just-in-time compilation.
nodes.hook: Compare time-to-first-execution with steady-state performance for a small numerical task.

nodes.name: Julia 1.0
nodes.note: Julia 1.0 established the stable 1.x language line.
nodes.hook: Explain how a 1.x compatibility commitment affects library authors.

nodes.name: Julia 1.12
nodes.note: Julia 1.12 was released in October 2025.
nodes.hook: Classify release changes as language, compiler, package manager or standard library.

nodes.name: Dynamic Application Languages
nodes.note: Ruby, Lua and Dart show contrasting server, embedded and application-development ecosystems.
nodes.hook: Match runtime, deployment target and tooling constraints to a suitable language.

nodes.name: Ruby
nodes.note: Ruby is a dynamic language with a mature server and automation ecosystem.
nodes.hook: Distinguish the Ruby language release from the Rails framework release.

nodes.name: Ruby 1.8
nodes.note: Ruby 1.8 was a widely used early production line.
nodes.hook: Find a compatibility issue that affected later migration.

nodes.name: Ruby 2.0
nodes.note: Ruby 2.0 began a long major-version period.
nodes.hook: Compare a major release promise with semantic versioning expectations.

nodes.name: Ruby 3.0
nodes.note: Ruby 3.0 introduced a new major release series.
nodes.hook: Evaluate performance claims using a workload relevant to the learner project.

nodes.name: Ruby 4.0
nodes.note: Ruby 4.0.0 was released on 25 December 2025.
nodes.hook: Read the release announcement and identify stable versus experimental features.

nodes.name: Lua
nodes.note: Lua is a compact embeddable language used in games and applications.
nodes.hook: Trace the boundary between a host application and embedded Lua scripts.

nodes.name: Lua 5.1
nodes.note: Lua 5.1 remains an important compatibility target in embedded ecosystems.
nodes.hook: Explain why embedded products may retain an older language version.

nodes.name: Lua 5.4
nodes.note: Lua 5.4 is the current official release series.
nodes.hook: Compare one 5.4 language change with 5.1 compatibility.

nodes.name: Dart
nodes.note: Dart is an application language closely associated with Flutter and multiple compilation targets.
nodes.hook: Draw the build path for a Dart mobile or web application.

nodes.name: Dart 1
nodes.note: Dart 1 established the initial stable language line.
nodes.hook: Identify how early optional typing differed from later sound typing.

nodes.name: Dart 2
nodes.note: Dart 2 made a sound static type system central to the language.
nodes.hook: Use a small example to show a compile-time type failure.

nodes.name: Dart 3
nodes.note: Dart 3 continued sound null safety and modern language features.
nodes.hook: Check the minimum SDK constraint before adopting a Dart 3 feature.

nodes.name: Functional and JVM Alternatives
nodes.note: Haskell, Scala and Clojure expose functional ideas through different runtime and type-system choices.
nodes.hook: Implement the same transformation in two branches and compare state, types and runtime.

nodes.name: Haskell 98
nodes.note: Haskell 98 defined a standardised lazy functional-language baseline.
nodes.hook: Explain purity and lazy evaluation using one traceable expression.

nodes.name: Haskell 2010
nodes.note: Haskell 2010 is the later published language report.
nodes.hook: Separate report-standard features from compiler extensions.

nodes.name: Scala 2
nodes.note: Scala 2 combined object-oriented and functional programming on the JVM.
nodes.hook: Compare Scala bytecode deployment with Java deployment.

nodes.name: Scala 3
nodes.note: Scala 3 revised the language while retaining the JVM ecosystem.
nodes.hook: Use migration guidance to classify source and binary compatibility risks.

nodes.name: Clojure 1.x
nodes.note: Clojure is a hosted Lisp whose main implementation targets the JVM.
nodes.hook: Compare immutable data and managed references with conventional mutable state.

nodes.name: Shell and Automation Languages
nodes.note: Bash and PowerShell combine language features with operating-system command ecosystems.
nodes.hook: Write the same file-management task safely in both shells and compare object versus text pipelines.

nodes.name: GNU Bash 5.x
nodes.note: Bash 5.x is a current major shell line across Unix-like systems.
nodes.hook: Audit quoting, globbing and exit-code handling in a deployment script.

nodes.name: PowerShell 7
nodes.note: PowerShell 7 is the cross-platform modern PowerShell line.
nodes.hook: Compare an object pipeline with a text pipeline and identify data-loss risks.

edges.note: TypeScript is checked and transformed into JavaScript for execution.
C++ developed from C but is a distinct standardised language.
Kotlin commonly targets the JVM alongside Java.
Useful comparison of managed application platforms.
Dart can compile applications for JavaScript-based web deployment.
